Header: Date: 2026-05-14 Time: 15:00 UTC Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam Ortiz (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (Oxbridge - Head of ML), Daniel Kim (Oxbridge - Platform Eng), Sara Martín (Oxbridge - CTO)

Auto-summary (auto-generated): Quick Optimize walkthrough focusing on batching and KV/prefix caching to reduce per-token cost. Discussed throughput targets, average seq lengths, cache hit-rate assumptions, and a simple cost model showing ~30-50% token cost savings depending on workload. Next steps: pricing, benchmark plan, sample prompts.

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Maya from Redwood, this is Liam, our SE. Today we're gonna run through Redwood Optimize recommendations for batching and KV/prefix cache and show a simple cost model for your payment flows.

[00:22] Priya: Thanks, Maya. Quick context — we run inference for transaction enrichment and fraud chat summarization. Peak QPS about 150 requests, avg tokens in prompt 220, responses ~120 tokens, we have both short and long tails. Latency SLOs around 350ms p95 for the enrichment path.

[00:45] Liam: Got it. That mix matters for batching and cache. For enrichment, you probably have a lot of repeated prefixes — customer metadata, instructions, system prompts — that's where prefix caching or a KV cache helps.

[01:10] Daniel: When you say prefix cache, is that different from the KV cache you demoed in the doc? Sometimes the terms get mixed in our notes.

[01:20] Liam: Yeah, sorry — our terminology is a bit messy in transcripts. Prefix cache is when we store the tokenized KV state for repeated prefixes so we don't re-run the prefix attention; KV cache is the runtime key-value cache within the model's attention that gets checkpointed between tokens. In Redwood Optimize we mean two levers: prefix-level caching (persisted per prompt template) and runtime KV reuse across calls when applicable.

[01:50] Sara: Okay, and how big are the savings realisticly? Our finance team will want numbers.

[01:58] Maya: Totally. We'll walk through a simple cost model. On a baseline hosted model at our standard latencies, without caching and minimal batching, your cost per response is X tokens * unit price. With batching and prefix cache we typically see 30-50% reduction depending on hit rate and batch size. For your profile — avg 220+120 tokens — with a 60% prefix hit and 6x batching at peak we estimate ~42% reduction.

[02:35] Priya: Where does quantization come in? We looked at some on-prem options previously and they touted 8-bit quantized models for cost delta.

[02:45] Liam: Quantization is orthogonal but complementary. If you run dedicated or private with quantized variants, you can cut base per-token op cost further. Optimize will recommend quantization based on your quality tests. For hosted, we lean on model variants that are already quant-friendly.

[03:08] Maya: We'll show the dashboard in a sec — the Optimize module gives suggested batch sizes, cache TTLs, and an estimated ROI line for each suggestion.

[03:20] [Screen share starts — Redwood Console - Optimize tab]

[03:35] Liam: Here is a sample workload profile — seq length distribution, tail, and token density. The key knobs: target latency SLO, max batch latency, and cache TTL. If you push batching too high you increase p95, so there's a tradeoff.

[04:05] Daniel: For enrichment path, p95 350ms — what's safe for batch delay?

[04:12] Liam: For a 350ms SLO, we usually cap batch wait at 60-80ms and rely on continuous batching to fill slots. That gives 4-8x effective batching at peak without breaking p95.

[04:30] Priya: Can we see the cost table?

[04:33] Liam: Yep. Baseline: no cache, minimal batching (batch=1), per-token compute cost roughly $0.000012 (example) — your monthly spend estimate for 150 QPS average would be $Y. If we add prefix caching with 60% hit, and modest batching (avg effective batch=5), compute cost drops to about 58% of baseline. These numbers are illustrative; we'll run an actual benchmark.

[05:05] Sara: Does the cache store PII? We have strict data residency and redaction rules.

[05:13] Maya: Good call — Redwood supports configurable cache scopes. Prefix caches are template-level and should avoid storing per-user PII. For KV caches that might include context, we can apply redaction hooks or opt out. On Private we support customer-managed KMS and retention policies.

[05:42] Priya: Are audit logs available for cache hits/misses? Our compliance team needs that.

[05:48] Liam: Yes, Console exposes hit/miss metrics and trace IDs; we also surface token-level cost attribution and can export logs to your SIEM. We have SOC 2 controls around logs, and we can include those artifacts in the security pack.

[06:10] Daniel: How does eviction work? We have ephemeral templates and some long-lived prompts.

[06:16] Liam: Eviction is TTL and LRUHybrid — you can tune TTLs per-template and set max entries. For long-lived templates you might want TTLs of 24h, for ephemeral flows TTL of a few minutes. Also you can pin templates for guaranteed retention (useful for high-value cached prefixes).

[06:42] Priya: If we do a pilot, what does bench plan look like?

[06:47] Maya: We'll run a 2-week pilot: week 1 — baseline collection (your traffic replay or sample), week 2 — enable recommended batching & prefix cache, run A/B to measure cost, latency, and quality. Liam will draft the test harness and perf scripts.

[07:05] [08:30] Liam: A couple of gotchas: prefix cache hit-rate depends on how much of the request is stable. If you include dynamic timestamps or ephemeral IDs in the seed text, hit-rate collapses. So one optimization is template normalization — strip IDs, replace with placeholders.

[08:45] Daniel: We do a lot of meta tokens from internal tracking, so we'll need to normalize. Good to know.

[09:05] Maya: Another lever is partial prompt caching — cache the large system instructions and only regen the last n tokens per-call. Works well if the system block is big.

[09:24] Priya: Any limitations on model types — does this work equally on decoder-only vs. chat-transformer variants?

[09:30] Liam: Mostly decoder-only and chat variants that expose KV can use runtime KV. Prefix-level caching is model-agnostic as long as the tokenizer and architecture are supported by the runtime. Optimize flags incompatible variants.

[10:05] Sara: Security question — we need SSO + SAML and strict RBAC so only platform eng can toggle cache policy. Is that in Console?

[10:12] Maya: Yes, Console supports SAML SSO, fine-grained RBAC, and audit trails for config changes. For Private deployments you can also lock config changes behind admin approval.

[10:40] Priya: Can you describe the expected perf improvement in tail latency when we use caching?

[10:47] Liam: Caching reduces compute per-request which reduces queuing; in our internal tests we've seen p95 drop by 20-35% on cached traffic under load. Combined with batching, you often see p50 drop a bit and p95 improve significantly because heavy requests are offloaded.

[11:20] Daniel: What about statefulness? Some of our flows require session state across calls. Does caching break anything?

[11:28] Liam: You can scope caches per-session or globally. For session state we recommend keeping session-specific small KV entries and not caching user-specific sensitive parts. You can also configure strict cache keys so only the stable parts are used as the cache key.

[12:05] Maya: I'll walk through the cost model spreadsheet quickly — high level: inputs are QPS, avg prompt tokens, avg response tokens, cache hit rate, effective batch size, model unit price. Then the sheet computes tokens saved and cost delta.

[12:30] [Screen: cost sheet — showing formulas]

[13:00] Liam: Example row: baseline tokens 340 per call => X tokens/mo. With prefix hit 60% (saves avg 120 tokens on hit) and batch size 5, effective calls per token drop; overall cost cut ~42% in that cell.

[13:35] Priya: How confident are those hit-rate assumptions? Ours might be lower, like 30%.

[13:42] Maya: If hit-rate is 30% and batch=3, savings drop to ~18-22%. That's why the pilot is important to get real numbers. Optimize also simulates hit-rates based on a sample set if you upload it.

[14:05] Daniel: Uploading data — is that secure? We have PII concerns.

[14:10] Maya: You can scrub PII client-side before upload. Alternatively we do a privacy-preserving sample run in your VPC for Private deployments.

[14:30] Priya: For the pilot, we want both hosted and a dedicated pilot comparison; finance will ask about committed capacity pricing.

[14:38] Maya: We can do a side-by-side: hosted pilot vs. small dedicated pool with reserved pricing. Liam can sketch the cost/latency tradeoff. Typically Dedicated yields predictable latency and better throughput per-dollar when you commit.

[15:05] Liam: One more technical note: we support adaptive batching — runtime adjusts batch sizes based on observed latency and queue fill. That helps keep p95 in-check while maximizing throughput.

[15:40] [20:00] Priya: Any integration effort — how quickly can we test?

[20:06] Maya: Integration is simple — our SDK + a short shim for normalization. End-to-end bench can be up in 3-5 days depending on your team bandwidth.

[21:15] Daniel: Is there an instrumentation hook we can push into our telemetry to track token-level cost per route?

[21:22] Liam: Yes — we expose per-route token and cost breakdowns plus a small tracing header you can attach so logs correlate with your internal traces.

[22:05] Sara: What are common pitfalls customers hit?

[22:12] Liam: Biggest are: accidentally including dynamic IDs in cache key, setting TTLs too long for ephemeral templates leading to stale outputs, and over-batching where median looks great but p95 balloons. We help with presets tuned to common workloads.

[23:00] Priya: Let's talk security docs — can you send SOC 2 and architecture diagram?

[23:06] Maya: Yes, we'll attach our security pack and an architecture diagram for hosted vs private.

[24:00] [30:00] Maya: Quick recap and next steps — Maya to send pricing and suggested sizing, Liam to share benchmark plan and perf scripts, Priya to provide sample prompt set and traffic profile. We'll schedule pilot kickoff for week of 2026-05-25.

[30:30] Priya: Sounds good. One last: do you have references in payments/fintech?

[30:40] Maya: We do — we can share anonymized case studies and a contact on a finance customer who ran a similar pilot.

[31:10] Daniel: Competitors — we're also talking to Vertex and evaluating Anthropic; any direct differentiators?

[31:18] Maya: Differentiators are production-first telemetry, first-class caching/batching knobs in Console, and predictable routing for Dedicated/Private. We also have cost-aware defaults tuned for finance flows.

[31:45] Sara: Okay thanks everyone.

[31:50] Maya: Thanks, we'll follow up with the docs and the bench plan.

[32:05] (End)
